scenario: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis vomits blood. Pressure is 88/50 and the heart rate is 120. He is resuscitated. A classmate orders only a proton-pump inhibitor and a clinic endoscopy next month.
question: Which drug is added now, and when is banding done?
options: Only a proton-pump inhibitor and a scope next month
A large-volume paracentesis as the bleeding treatment
Octreotide plus an antibiotic, then urgent banding
Observation, because cirrhosis vomit is gastritis until a month has passed
correctAnswer: Octreotide plus an antibiotic, then urgent banding
explanation:
Suspected variceal bleeding is treated with a vasoactive drug such as octreotide, an antibiotic, and urgent endoscopy for banding. A proton-pump inhibitor alone is not enough. Variceal bleeding needs a splanchnic constrictor, infection prophylaxis, and endoscopy now. A delayed clinic scope misses the bleed. Laine L, Barkun AN, Saltzman JR, Martel M, Leontiadis GI. ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2021.

Octreotide plus an antibiotic, then urgent banding
Only a proton-pump inhibitor and a scope next month — The bleed needs treatment today.
Beta blockade during active hematemesis — A beta blocker is prevention after the bleed is controlled, not the first act while hypotensive.
A large-volume paracentesis as the bleeding treatment — Paracentesis treats tense ascites, not hematemesis.
Observation, because cirrhosis vomit is gastritis until a month has passed — Hypotension means an urgent source.
citation: Laine L, Barkun AN, Saltzman JR, Martel M, Leontiadis GI. ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2021.
